list.listitem: Monitor all pregnancies for fetal growth. C
The USPSTF recommends low dose aspirin for women at risk for pre-eclampsia to reduce the likelihood of intrauterine growth restriction (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.68-0.99). A
Evaluate pregnancies complicated by maternal disease, maternal risk factors, or concerning fetal growth by ultrasonography. B
Perform Doppler ultrasound assessment of umbilical artery waveforms once intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is suspected or diagnosed (associated with a decrease in perinatal death). A
Institute antepartum surveillance in growth-restricted fetuses. C
Small for gestational age (SGA) infants are at risk for perinatal morbidity and mortality, short stature, developmental delays, and a variety of adult diseases. B

background.definition: SGA implies fetal or birth weight less than the 10th percentile. SGA fetuses and neonates can be constitutionally small (size genetically appropriate) or pathologically small (having IUGR, also known as fetal growth restriction). IUGR implies a decreased rate of growth in utero; these fetuses/neonates are usually SGA, but IUGR can also include those with a drop in growth rate who are still above the 10th percentile.

list.listitem: Ten percent of fetuses are SGA; 50% to 70% of these are constitutionally small.
Three percent to 5% of all pregnancies show IUGR (120,000-200,000 pregnancies per year in the United States).

An association between SGA and development later in life of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, coronary heart disease, impaired glucose tolerance, and diabetes suggests that the impact of IUGR may extend into adulthood.

Maternal associations: hypertension (chronic or pregnancy induced), uterine abnormalities, diabetes, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and thrombophilias, collagen vascular disease, thrombocytopenia, renal disease, restrictive lung disease, cyanotic heart disease, hemoglobinopathies, severe malnutrition, and infections.
Socioeconomic risk factors: cigarette smoking, substance use (particularly methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, alcohol, and methadone).
Placental factors: multiple gestations, villitis, infarcts, previa, chronic abruption, vasculitis, thrombosis, chorioangioma, abnormal cord insertion, and circumvallate.
Fetal factors: chromosomal anomalies, metabolic disorders, genetic syndromes, infections (cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella), and teratogens.
Risk factors for IUGR: shown below in the Risk Factor section, the most important being black race and tobacco use.
Symmetric IUGR (both head and body show decreased growth) usually starts early in pregnancy and is generally the result of intrinsic factors affecting the fetus directly.

Asymmetric IUGR (head growth relatively normal) usually starts in mid to late pregnancy and is generally the result of extrinsic factors affecting uterine perfusion or the placenta. Decreased nutrient and oxygen delivery, limited growth-promoting hormones, and inhibition of nitric oxide production are likely mechanisms.
The causes of IUGR are also common causes of preterm labor; thus, many premature infants are SGA.
Monitor all pregnancies for fetal growth. B
Evaluate pregnancies complicated by maternal disease, maternal risk factors, or concerning fetal growth by ultrasonography. B
The USPSTF recommends low dose aspirin for women at risk for pre-eclampsia reduced the likelihood of intrauterine growth restriction (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.68-0.99). A
The USPSTF recommends that women should be screened for pre-eclampsia with blood pressure measurements throughout pregnancy.
Screen all pregnancies routinely for IUGR using clinical techniques (eg, serial fundal height measurements).
Perform ultrasonography for patients with maternal disease, risk factors for IUGR, or concerning clinical presentation.
Evaluate further when the fetal size is less than the 10th percentile based on estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference (see ).

A large randomized trial in the Netherlands found that while routine screening USN in the 3rd trimester increased detection of small for gestational age fetuses, there was no difference in neonatal or perinatal outcomes.
It has been estimated that 14% of IUGR would be eliminated if smoking could be completely prevented during pregnancy.

Aspirin in low doses (aspirin >100 mg daily was more effective than 60 mg daily (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31-0.74)), particularly when initiated prior to 16 weeks gestation, decreases the risk of pre-eclapsia, preterm birth, and IUGR in women at high risk for pre-eclampsia.
Enoxaparin does not reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia and IUGR in women at high risk for pre-eclampsia.
Omega-3 fatty acids do not reduce the risk of IUGR.
The risk of IUGR in subsequent pregnancies is determined by the underlying cause of poor fetal growth. Interventions based on the underlying disease process may be helpful in improving fetal growth.
Perform Doppler ultrasound assessment of umbilical artery waveforms once IUGR is suspected or diagnosed (associated with a decrease in perinatal death). B
Evaluate the placenta grossly and microscopically following every unexplained SGA or IUGR delivery. C
Use the history (including parental stature) and physical examination to guide the diagnostic evaluation of SGA infants. C
Measure the weight, length, and head circumference carefully; these are essential for evaluating the small neonate.
Calculation of the ponderal index is helpful (100 times the birth weight in grams divided by the cubed birth length in centimeters).
Plot the weight, length, head circumference, and ponderal index against the estimated gestational age.
Birth weight less than the 10th percentile with normal ponderal index suggests symmetric IUGR or constitutional SGA.
Birth weight less than the 10th percentile with low ponderal index suggests asymmetric IUGR.
Look for stigmata of congenital infection (hepatosplenomegaly, blueberry muffin rash, petechiae, cataracts, abnormal hearing screen) and any dysmorphic features.
Parental heights are essential to the diagnosis of constitutional SGA.
The biophysical profile is highly correlated with umbilical venous cord pH. It is a good predictor of still birth and less predictive of adverse outcome.
Doppler ultrasonography of the umbilical artery is the best tool for identifying the small fetus at risk.
Doppler ultrasonography of multiple vessels (eg, umbilical artery, middle cerebral artery, ductus venosus, and inferior vena cava) demonstrates the degree of placental insufficiency.
Fetal blood sampling is now used less frequently because of the efficacy of Doppler ultrasound and the risk of the procedure.
Perform gross and microscopic evaluation of the placenta in all unexplained cases of SGA or IUGR.
For recommended diagnostic testing of the neonate after birth, see .
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.

Vitamin or mineral supplementation, plasma volume expansion, maternal oxygen, antihypertensives, heparin, and aspirin therapy have not been shown to be effective for the prevention or treatment of IUGR. B
Institute antepartum surveillance once the possibility of extrauterine survival for the growth-restricted fetus has been determined. C
Treat any infections.
Give betamethasone for preterm labor.
Give intrapartum antibiotics for known group B Streptococcus colonization or unknown group B Streptococcus status.

In women with antiphospholipid syndrome and recurrent miscarriages, or in women with a history of IUGR, aspirin and anticoagulants are often recommended, but good studies are lacking to support this practice.
An RCT of 118 women with IUGR between 22 and 29 weeks showed sildenafil did not affect growth velocity compared to placebo.
Avoidance of smoking, alcohol, and illicit substances.

Institute antepartum surveillance once the possibility of extrauterine survival for the growth-restricted fetus has been determined. This may include Doppler velocimetry, contraction stress testing, a nonstress test with amniotic fluid volume assessment, and a biophysical profile.

A systematic review found little evidence regarding specific strategies. One RCT with 167 women found no difference in clinical outcomes between groups evaluated twice a week compared with once every 2 weeks, other than more labor inductions in the group surveilled more frequently.
Delivery when risks of continuation of pregnancy outweigh the benefits.

Treatments not recommended for IUGR due to insufficient evidence or questionable efficacy: bed rest, nutritional supplements, maternal oxygen therapy, plasma volume expansion, heparin, low-dose aspirin, and vaginal sildenafil.
Perinatology referral recommended for pregnancies with IUGR, particularly for surveillance and timing of delivery.

Refer SGA children with short stature persisting beyond 3 years of age (height >2 SD below the mean for chronologic age) to a pediatrician who has expertise in endocrinology for full evaluation and consideration of growth hormone therapy.
SGA infants are at increased risk for perinatal morbidity and mortality (eg, acidosis, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, polycythemia, sepsis, coagulopathy, intraventricular hemorrhage, death). B

Most studies report that SGA infants are at increased risk for short stature and developmental delays. SGA infants born premature or with fetal circulatory redistribution with preferential perfusion of the brain are at increased risk for developmental delays. B

A systematic review of 60 studies with 52,822 children found that children born with intrauterine growth restriction who were SGA had significantly worse cognitive outcomes than term infants (SMD -0.39, 95% CI -0.50 to -0.28).B

However, a prospective cohort study of 174 children with fetal growth restriction due to early onset placental insufficiency found that these fetal growth restricted children had height and BMI scores comparable to their age-matched peers at 12.5 years of age.B
SGA infants are at increased risk for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, coronary heart disease, impaired glucose tolerance, and diabetes. B
IUGR is the most important fetal predictor of sudden intrauterine unexplained death (OR 7.0; 95% CI 3.3-15.1). B

Fetuses with early onset growth restriction and umbilical artery absent end-diastolic velocities (OR 3.6), umbilical artery reversed end-diastolic velocities (OR 7.3), and ductus venosus absent or reversed end-diastolic velocities (OR 11.6) are at increased risk of death.B

Neonatal Status Diagnostic Testing
Constitutional SGA Not likely to be helpful
Dysmorphic features Chromosomal analysis, genetics consultation
Symmetric IUGR or physical findings of intrauterine infection IgM serology for toxoplasma/CMV/rubella, urine for CMV, cranial ultrasound
Asymmetric IUGR Cord blood IgM and urine for CMV
